lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Tiresias — if you're still blind, there's really no way of telling anymore. The eye-sockets are empty on all of us; only the holes are left. You couldn't say at this point which one of us is Phineus and which one is Lynceus. But I do know you were a prophet, and I know you were the only person ever to be both a man and a woman — I've heard the poets on the subject. So in the gods' name, tell me: which of the two lives did you find more pleasant? Was being a man better, or was the woman's side of things the improvement?
lines.description: curious deadpan, anatomical joke landing lightly before probing

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: By a long way, Menippus — the woman's. Less trouble. The women run the men, and they don't have to go to war, or stand a watch on the ramparts, or argue in the assembly, or get cross-examined in the courts.
lines.description: authoritative, matter-of-fact; enjoying the decisive answer

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: You haven't heard Euripides' Medea, then, Tiresias? The speech where she pities the female condition — wretched creatures, she calls them, bearing the unbearable agony of childbirth? [pause] Which actually reminds me — Medea's lines just put it in my head — when you were a woman, did you ever give birth? Or did you go through that whole stretch of life barren and childless?
lines.description: pleasantly forensic; the pause pivots into awkward specificity

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: Why are you asking me this, Menippus?
lines.description: guarded, suspicious, dignity beginning to tighten

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Nothing difficult about it, Tiresias. Just answer the question, if it's not too much trouble.
lines.description: mild and polite, but relentless underneath

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I wasn't barren. But I never actually had a child.
lines.description: reluctant precision, trying to end the matter quickly

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: That'll do. But did you have a womb? That's what I wanted to know.
lines.description: brisk, delighted by the absurdly practical follow-up

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.description: stiff, offended, forced into blunt admission

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And over time the womb just — disappeared? And the female parts sealed themselves shut, and the breasts dropped off, and the male equipment sprouted, and you grew a beard? Or did you flip from woman to man all at once?
lines.description: clinical curiosity, escalating list with dry comic precision

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: I don't see what you're driving at with these questions. You seem not to believe it happened the way it happened.
lines.description: defensive authority, irritation held behind formality

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Well, ought one not to disbelieve a story like that, Tiresias? Should one just swallow it whole, like some half-wit, without examining whether the thing is actually possible?
lines.description: reasonable tone, quietly cutting; philosopher as fact-checker

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: So you don't believe any of the rest of it either, when you hear that women turned into birds or trees or wild animals — Aëdon, or Daphne, or the daughter of Lycaon?
lines.description: indignant, reaching for mythic precedent as evidence

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: If I ever run into any of them, I'll find out what they have to say for themselves. [pause] But you, my friend — when you were a woman, were you already a prophet then, the way you were later? Or did you become a man and a seer at the same moment?
lines.description: dryly practical, then friendly pivot to another trap

lines.speaker: Tiresias
lines.text: There — you see? You don't know the first thing about my story. I settled a dispute among the gods, and Hera maimed me for it, and Zeus consoled me for the disaster with the gift of prophecy.
lines.description: wounded pride, reciting official legend with solemn authority

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Still at it with the tall tales, Tiresias? [chuckles] Well — that's prophets for you. It's a professional habit. None of you can manage a straight word.
lines.description: affectionately dismissive; chuckle dry, final verdict lands flat
